planting.note: Plant seeds or divisions in spring in lean, well-drained, dry sandy or rocky soil in full sun to light shade; this sprawling, semi-woody aster is native to dry pine-oak sandhills and open woodlands of the Coastal Plain and Piedmont from North Carolina to Florida and Louisiana and resents rich, moist, or heavily amended soil.

directions: Set out plants or divisions in spring into lean, dry, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full sun to light shade, allowing room for the sprawling, semi-woody stems to spread and scramble through neighboring plants. This is one of the largest-flowered native asters, opening abundant lavender-purple, yellow-centered blooms very late in the season, often continuing into November after most other asters have finished, making it an exceptional last-chance nectar source for migrating monarchs and late-flying bees. It thrives on neglect in dry sandhills and open pinelands and declines quickly in fertile or consistently damp garden soil, so pair it with other dry-site natives rather than average perennial border plants. Cut back hard in late winter to tidy the woody framework before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant seeds or divisions in spring in dry, infertile, sandy soil in full sun; scaleleaf aster is a diminutive Gulf and southern Atlantic Coastal Plain species of sandy pinelands and sandhills, with small, scale-like leaves pressed close to wiry stems.

directions: Plant in spring into dry, sandy, low-fertility soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since individuals are slender and wiry-stemmed. The small, scale-like leaves clasp tightly along the stems, giving the plant a fine, almost heath-like texture quite different from the broad-leaved asters of moist woodlands, and it is well suited to sandhill, longleaf pine, and dune-margin plantings across the Gulf and lower Atlantic Coastal Plain. Numerous small pale blue to violet flowers open in loose sprays in fall, drawing small native bees and other short-tongued pollinators. Avoid irrigation and rich soil amendments, which quickly cause this dry-site specialist to weaken and rot.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in dry to average, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; creeping aster is a low, rhizomatous groundcover restricted to the Piedmont of the Carolinas and Georgia, spreading steadily by underground stems to form dense colonies in open woodland.

directions: Set divisions in spring in dry to average, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun, spacing plants to allow the spreading rhizomes to knit together into a groundcover over a season or two. Unlike most woodland asters, this low, mat-forming species stays under two feet tall even in bloom, with wiry stems carrying pale lavender, thin-rayed flowers above small, leathery basal leaves in fall. Its narrow native range in the dry oak-pine Piedmont of North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia makes it uncommon in commerce, but it is an effective, low-maintenance native substitute for non-native groundcovers on dry slopes and woodland edges. Divide congested colonies every few years to maintain vigor and share with other gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow seed in fall in dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; twisted-leaf goldenrod is a slender Coastal Plain species of sandhills and dry pinelands from North Carolina to Florida and Alabama, named for its narrow leaves that twist slightly along their length.

directions: Sow seed in fall directly into dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; this narrow-leaved goldenrod is adapted to the fire-maintained sandhills and dry pineland understory of the lower Southeast and struggles in heavier or richer garden soils. Slender stems carry narrow leaves with a distinctive slight twist, topped in fall by an open, branching spray of small golden flower heads that is less dense than many showier garden goldenrods but well suited to naturalistic dry-meadow and pine savanna plantings. It supports the same broad range of fall-migrating bees, wasps, and butterflies as other Coastal Plain goldenrods without the aggressive spread of some rhizomatous species. Leave seed heads standing through winter for songbirds before cutting back in late winter.
